hops.afterHeading: Count before you divide: homologs, sisters and ploidy
hops.title: Two look-alike deer with 46 and 6 chromosomes
hops.text: Muntjacs are small Asian deer, also called barking deer. The Chinese muntjac and the Indian muntjac look alike, and they can mate and have live hybrid fawns. Now count their centromeres. The Chinese muntjac has 46 chromosomes in both sexes, the same number as you. The Indian muntjac has 6 in females and 7 in males: in its line, ancestral chromosomes fused into a few giant ones. Yet the two species carry similar amounts of DNA per haploid set, 2.7 picograms in the Chinese muntjac and 2.1 in the Indian. A chromosome count tells you how the DNA is packaged, not how much there is.

sources.citation: Tsipouri et al., Genome Biology 9(10):R155 (2008), PMC2760882.

image.caption: Chinese and Indian muntjacs look alike and hold similar DNA, yet carry 46 versus 6 or 7 chromosomes.

hops.afterHeading: Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sisters
hops.title: Why a supermarket banana has no seeds
hops.text: Next time you peel a banana, snap it in half and look down the middle. Those tiny brown flecks are the remains of ovules, the structures that would have become seeds. Wild bananas are diploid, and their fruit is packed with hard, gravelly seeds. Cavendish and most other dessert bananas are triploid: three sets of 11, or 33 chromosomes. At anaphase I, three homologs cannot split evenly between two poles, so meiosis often makes gametes with unbalanced sets. That, with sterility genes and rearranged chromosomes, means seeds rarely form. The fruit grows anyway, without fertilization, and growers propagate the plants as clones.

sources.citation: Heslop-Harrison & Schwarzacher, Annals of Botany 100(5):1073-1084 (2007), PMC2759213.
Miao et al., Horticulture Research 12(5):uhaf044 (2025), PMC11997438.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Hands breaking a peeled yellow banana in half over a wooden counter, showing tiny brown specks in the center.
image.caption: The brown flecks are ovules that never became seeds; three chromosome sets help keep Cavendish bananas seedless.

hops.afterHeading: Crossing over: what holds the pair, and what it does to alleles
hops.title: A Romanian jawbone with a recent Neanderthal ancestor
hops.text: In 2002, a human jawbone turned up in a Romanian cave called Peștera cu Oase. It is 37,000 to 42,000 years old. When geneticists read its DNA in 2015, they estimated that 6 to 9 percent was Neanderthal, far more than the 1 to 3 percent in present-day Eurasians, and some Neanderthal stretches were unusually long. Crossing over swaps pieces between non-sister chromatids, so over the generations, long stretches from any one ancestor tend to get broken up. From those long stretches, the team estimated a Neanderthal ancestor four to six generations back, less than 200 years before this man lived: possibly as close as a great-great-grandparent.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A weathered fossil lower jawbone on dark linen beside a small wooden brush and a brass magnifying glass.
image.caption: In 2015, long Neanderthal stretches in an ancient Romanian jawbone suggested a Neanderthal ancestor four to six generations back.

audio.title: Sibling DNA, fatherless condor chicks and a Neanderthal ancestor
audio.transcript:
Meiosis can feel like pure bookkeeping: count the centromeres, pair the homologs, pull them apart. But that bookkeeping shows up in some odd places. Here are three.

First, your siblings. Full brothers and sisters are said to share half their D N A. That means something specific: along their chromosomes, the two of them inherited the very same parental copy about half the time. It sounds like it should be exactly half. You got one set of chromosomes from each parent, and so did your sister. But you and your sister came from different eggs and different sperm, made in separate rounds of meiosis. In each meiosis, every chromosome pair lines up on the spindle in a random orientation, and crossing over swaps segments between the homologs before they part. So two siblings are two separate samples from the same two parents. In two thousand six, researchers used genetic markers to track which parental copies four thousand four hundred and one pairs of full siblings had inherited, across the twenty-two pairs of non-sex chromosomes. On average, the siblings had the same parental copy for forty-nine point eight percent of their genome. Right on half. But real pairs ranged from thirty-seven point four percent all the way up to sixty-one point seven. Most pairs sat within a few percent of half. Still, if you have two siblings, you probably share a little more of your inheritance with one of them than with the other.

Second, a mystery from the California condor recovery program. By nineteen eighty-two, only twenty-two California condors were left, so conservation geneticists tracked the population closely. In two thousand twenty-one, they reported on nine hundred eleven genotyped condors, and two male chicks stood out. The genetic markers ruled out every possible father. At all twenty-one sites tested, each chick carried two copies of one of its mother's versions. And neither mother was single. One had already produced eleven chicks with her mate. The other had been paired with her mate for twenty years and had produced twenty-three chicks with him before she laid a fatherless egg. She has since had two more chicks with him. In birds, males carry two Z chromosomes, and both chicks were Z Z males. The researchers said the pattern fits an unfertilized egg that, after meiosis, either doubled its single set or fused with another product of the same meiosis. They could not tell which.

Third, crossing over as a clock. In two thousand two, a human jawbone turned up in a cave in Romania. It is thirty-seven thousand to forty-two thousand years old. When geneticists read its D N A in two thousand fifteen, six to nine percent of it was Neanderthal. Present-day Eurasians carry one to three percent. And three of the Neanderthal stretches were huge and unbroken. Here is why that matters. When crossing over swaps pieces between non-sister chromatids, it can break up stretches inherited from an ancestor, so over the generations, long stretches tend to get cut down. Several stretches that long point to recent ancestry. The researchers estimated that this man's Neanderthal ancestor lived only four to six generations before him, less than two hundred years earlier. That ancestor could have been as close as a great-great-grandparent.

Same machinery, three stories: random draws that make siblings differ, an egg that found its own second set, and crossing over that keeps time.
